---
title: "The EPPF: why the order of arrival does not matter"
subtitle: "Catalog P-14 · rung 6 · after Broderick (MLSS 2016, part II; 2012 tutorial)"
description: "The probability of a seating is a product of Chinese restaurant factors, and every arrival order gives the same product."
toc: false
---

Seat eight customers by the [Chinese restaurant rule](crp.qmd) and end with the tables
{1, 2, 7, 8}, {3, 5, 6} and {4}. The probability of that seating is a product of one factor
per customer: alpha/(alpha + n − 1) when customer n opens a table, m/(alpha + n − 1) when
it joins a table of m. The numerators collect alpha once per table and (|C| − 1)! for each
table C; the denominators are the same in any order. So the product is the *exchangeable
partition probability function*

P(Π_N) = alpha^K ∏_C (|C| − 1)! / ∏_{n = 1}^{N} (alpha + n − 1),

which depends only on the table sizes.

## What to try

- **Shuffle arrival order** (or Enter). The factors under the customers change; the product
  does not. At alpha = 1 it is 1/3360 = .000298 in every order.
- **alpha.** All orders still agree, now at a different value.
- **New seating** draws another partition of eight customers from the restaurant;
  **Broderick's example** brings back {1, 2, 7, 8}, {3, 5, 6}, {4}.
- **The exercise** below the panel asks for E[K_8], the expected number of tables, and
  checks the answer with the engine.

Exchangeability is what lets a multisite analysis treat the units' labels as arbitrary:
only the sizes of the clusters carry information about alpha. The same product, summed
over all partitions with K tables, gives the prior pmf of K_J used everywhere on this site.
